title: Scoring Frameworks: RICE, ICE & Beyond
description: Learn how to apply RICE, ICE, and weighted scoring models to prioritize projects with confidence.

interactions.prompt: In the RICE framework, which factor measures how many people a feature will affect in a given time period?
interactions.teachingPreamble: RICE stands for Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort. It was popularized by Intercom to score product features. The formula is (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort, giving you a single score to compare projects.

interactions.prompt: Feature A: Reach 5,000, Impact 3, Confidence 80%, Effort 4 person-months. Feature B: Reach 12,000, Impact 2, Confidence 50%, Effort 3 person-months. Which has the higher RICE score?
How does the ICE framework differ most from RICE?

options.text: ICE uses revenue instead of reach
ICE replaces Reach with a simpler 1-10 scale approach
ICE adds a time-based urgency factor
ICE removes the confidence component entirely

interactions.teachingPreamble: ICE stands for Impact, Confidence, and Ease. Unlike RICE, it drops the Reach metric and scores each factor on a simple 1-10 scale. Sean Ellis at GrowthHackers created ICE for fast experimentation where you need quick, gut-informed scoring without detailed data.

interactions.prompt: In weighted scoring, you assign each criterion a ____ so that factors like revenue impact can count more heavily than ease of implementation.
Your startup has 6 weeks of runway pressure. You need to prioritize 20 feature ideas fast. Your data team says they need 2 weeks to gather Reach numbers for a proper RICE analysis. What do you use?

options.text: Wait for RICE data — precision matters most
Use ICE scoring now — speed beats precision here
Skip frameworks and let the CEO decide
Build a custom weighted model from scratch

interactions.prompt: A Shopify PM labels a checkout redesign as 'Must Have' and dark mode as 'Won't Have this time.' Which framework is she using?
interactions.teachingPreamble: MoSCoW categorizes items into Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, and Won't Have. Unlike numeric scoring, it groups work into priority buckets. It's especially popular in agile projects where teams need clear agreement on what's non-negotiable versus nice-to-have.

interactions.prompt: A fintech team uses weighted scoring (criteria: Revenue Impact 40%, Customer Retention 30%, Effort 30%). Rank these features highest to lowest priority: (a) Revenue 6, Retention 8, Effort 3; (b) Revenue 9, Retention 7, Effort 5; (c) Revenue 4, Retention 5, Effort 9; (d) Revenue 8, Retention 9, Effort 4.

Your competitor just launched a near-identical feature to your top-ranked item, eliminating its differentiation value. Your RICE score assumed high impact from being first-to-market. What should you do?

options.text: Ship it anyway — the RICE score still holds
Re-score the Impact and Confidence factors, then re-rank
Drop it entirely and start over with new ideas
Switch from RICE to MoSCoW to avoid the problem

interactions.priorContext: You previously ranked features using RICE and selected a top project based on first-mover advantage. Now a competitor has launched the same feature, fundamentally changing the Impact and Confidence assumptions in your original score.
